stories.topic: Landings in Burma vs. Landings in China
stories.summary: To open the toolkit, Ajay asks us to imagine a hypothetical Indian expeditionary force weighing amphibious landings in Burma against landings in China. We see at once that both are very hard. But a sufficiently complex naval operation could manage Burma, while China is practically impossible. He then asks whether we could make the same quick call about demands like manipulating the exchange rate, stabilising inflation, building an atom bomb, or polio vaccination.
stories.insight: We already make fast, calibrated 'easy vs. hard' judgments in some domains. The goal is to make that same move routine for policy proposals, so they are weighed on feasibility and not just desirability.
stories.quote: Watch what we just did. We discussed a problem statement and we arrived at a judgment that is this easy or is this hard.

stories.topic: The Op-ed Behind 'Monetary Policy is Easy, Financial Regulation is Hard'
stories.summary: Ajay calls the day he figured this out one of the happy days of his life. We tend to see central banking as one blur. But a modern monetary policy committee has five members, which he says should be the RBI governor plus four independent private economists. They meet six times a year to hit a 4% inflation target and each writes a public rationale. That makes it low on transactions, discretion, stakes and opacity. Financial regulation is the opposite. It means about a thousand firms and roughly 2,000 touch points a year, judgment calls on whether a loan is an NPA, billions of dollars that can make or break business models, and supervision done in secrecy. That is four on four.
stories.insight: Two activities that look alike to outsiders sit at opposite ends of the difficulty spectrum once you take them apart. A country like India can build an inflation-targeting system fairly easily. Banking regulation will always be hard, and even the United States suffers doing it.
stories.quote: So for all the hype and mystique around monetary policy, actually it's a trivial, easy problem. You need to get six decisions correct per year.

stories.topic: The Railway Ticket Clerk Who Could Lie
stories.summary: In the old days, the booking status of every seat on every train lived in a paper register inside the railway office. The clerk at the ticket window therefore had complete discretion and could simply claim there were no seats. Once the data moved into a database that the whole world can see, ideally through an open API, that discretion vanished: seat 2A is either taken or not. Ajay adds that the government needn't even run IRCTC. It only needs to open an API, and ClearTrip and MakeMyTrip will do the rest.
stories.insight: The real reform value of an IT system is not glamour. It is that it removes discretion from the frontline civil servant and so turns a hard component into an easy one.
stories.quote: He could lie to you, he could say there's no ticket here.

stories.topic: What Nehru Should Have Heard in 1947
stories.summary: After reading Adam Smith's line on peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice, Ajay imagines someone saying this to Jawaharlal Nehru in 1947. Nehru brushes it off: that's all good, but we also need land reform. The right answer, Ajay argues, would have been to take fright at how hard each of the three is and refuse everything else.
stories.insight: The essentials of statecraft are not modest chores you finish before the exciting projects. They are among the hardest problems there are, and taking on extra goals early robs them of scarce capability.
stories.quote: Wow, peace very hard. Easy taxes, very hard. Tolerable administration of justice, very hard. We have our hands full, we are swamped. Don't give me anything more to do.

stories.summary: A good policeman in a rule-of-law country finds a drunk man searching under a lamppost and helps him look for his key. Finding nothing, he asks where the key was dropped. 'Over there in the bushes where it's very dark.' Then why look here? 'Because this is where the light is.' Amit uses the parable against RCTs in development economics, which he used to open his Seen and the Unseen episode with Lant Pritchett. He later found Yuen Yuen Ang used the same metaphor, almost simultaneously, in her paper 'Adaptive Political Economy', and wrote to her about it.
stories.insight: Measurable, attributable problems tempt us because they let us feel productive, while the consequential problems stay fuzzy and in the dark. It is worth asking whether you are working on something because it matters or because it is well-lit.
stories.quote: RCTs are solving inconsequential, easy problems simply because they're attributable and measurable and it's a great fraud on the field of economics.

recommendations.item: Solutions When the Solution is the Problem: Arraying the Disarray in Development
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock
recommendations.context: The 2004 paper that first proposed two of the metrics, number of transactions and discretion. Ajay and Vijay Kelkar later built on it.
recommendations.reason: Ajay loves it because the question it asks, whether an intervention is easy or hard to implement, was itself a breakthrough. Indian policy debate rarely asks it.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Plugged while discussing Pritchett's framework. Amit also notes he opened that episode with the drunk-under-the-lamppost metaphor.
recommendations.reason: It is the longer conversation with the originator of the framework, including Amit's critique of RCTs as searching where the light is.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's most recent life-and-times conversation with Ajay, mentioned alongside the Pritchett episode.
recommendations.reason: It is the long-form version of Ajay's thinking. Ajay now has fourteen episodes on the show.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay cites 'Kelkar and Shah' for its section 'Everybody Loves a Good IT System'. He and Kelkar are also the ones who extended the Pritchett-Woolcock framework.
recommendations.reason: It is where the authors take apart the comfortable escape routes from hard state problems, such as celebrating a new IT system while nothing gets done.

recommendations.item: Monetary policy is easy; Financial regulation is hard
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The op-ed Ajay wrote when the contrast first clicked for him, which he calls one of the happy days of his life.
recommendations.reason: It is the original statement of the episode's central worked example: two 'central bank' jobs that differ sharply in difficulty.

recommendations.item: Improving governance using large IT systems
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's 2005 paper on the role of IT in governance, written while he was taken with the railway reservation system.
recommendations.reason: It argues that IT can tame high-transaction, high-discretion components and make a hard problem manageable.

recommendations.item: How to correctly draw the perimeter for government software systems (Big Ideas, Episode 20)
recommendations.context: Ajay says he will link a video when making the point that the government needn't run IRCTC itself.
recommendations.reason: It expands on the idea that the state should open up an API and let private players like ClearTrip and MakeMyTrip build on it.

recommendations.item: Adaptive Political Economy: Toward a New Paradigm
recommendations.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
recommendations.context: Amit found that Ang used the same lamppost metaphor almost simultaneously and wrote to her.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a fantastic paper by a great scholar who reached the same diagnosis on her own.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything's series on the state (Episodes 25, 26, 33, 91, 92, 99)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit flags this episode as part of a family covering understanding the state, when it should act, public choice theory, separation of powers, rules vs. discretion, and Indian regulation.
recommendations.reason: Each episode adds a separate concept without repeating, so together they form a complete toolkit for thinking about when and how the state should intervene.

recommendations.item: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Episode 67, EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay points to it while setting the conditions for 'easy' monetary policy: no currency trading and an open capital account.
recommendations.reason: Monetary policy is only easy if the exchange rate floats and the central bank sticks to inflation targeting. This episode explains that precondition.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's example of low transactions: a government handing out about 500 research grants a year.
recommendations.reason: It shows what a low-transaction state intervention looks like, in contrast to polio drops for 500 million people.

recommendations.creator: The Beatles
recommendations.context: Quoted while mocking ribbon-cutting government IT projects: 'Father McKenzie wiping the dirt from his hands as he walks from the grave. No one was saved.'
recommendations.reason: A beautiful song that, for Ajay, captures how he thinks about most government IT systems.

recommendations.creator: U2
recommendations.context: From the 1984 album The Unforgettable Fire.
recommendations.reason: One of two songs from that album he calls 'absolutely great'.

recommendations.reason: The second of his two picks from the album.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay gives four quick reasons for his and Amit's scepticism of the Indian state. (1) Information: society is too complex, so the true facts are unknowable to planners. (2) Public choice: the incentives of state personnel clash with the state's objectives. (3) Political economy: special interest groups push government behaviour around. (4) State capability: even well-meant projects get badly implemented. Hence their 'environment of diffidence' whenever someone says the government should do one more thing.
core_ideas.quote: The government is not a mythological creature of infinite capability. The government is a deeply flawed creature.

core_ideas.concept: Ask 'Is It Possible?', Not Just 'Is It Justified?'
core_ideas.explanation: Whether the state should intervene depends on whether it can succeed, not only on whether the goal is worthy. Implementation constraints belong at the start of any policy discussion. Mainstream Indian debate 'blithely runs forward' from values to action. If you first judge which goals are easy and which are hard, you can ration money and management effort, letting some lovely objectives go and taking on the ones you can actually win.
core_ideas.quote: when we think about public policy, we should always bring implementation constraints on the table. Like right up front, start thinking, can we do it? Do we have the ability to do it?

core_ideas.explanation: A proposed intervention gets harder the higher it scores on four tests. (1) Transactions: 500 research grants a year vs. polio drops for 500 million people. (2) Discretion of frontline workers: people use discretion in favour of friends, kin and self-interest. (3) Stakes: a policeman who can jail you vs. a vaccinator with nothing to gain. (4) Opacity: body cams, the CAG, RTI and published statistics let journalists, researchers and opposition parties criticise, while secrecy hands over raw arbitrary power. Pritchett and Woolcock proposed the first two, and Kelkar and Shah added stakes and opacity. Amit notes that all four probe the same gap between the state's objectives and its employees' incentives.
core_ideas.quote: We have a clear toolkit and you don't even need paper and pen. You can just memorize this.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay fills an imaginary table on the fly. Elementary schools score high on transactions and discretion (the teacher decides whether to teach, make eye contact, or try harder), but stakes are low (a modest salary) and opacity can be fixed: two out of four. HPV or polio vaccination involves high transactions but a fixed protocol, no stakes and full transparency, so it is easy. The judiciary has ultimate discretion and stakes, plus closed-door bench deliberations: three and a half out of four. Taxation has huge numbers of transactions, high officer discretion, stakes of thousands of crores and full opacity: four on four.
core_ideas.quote: Taxation. High number of transactions, high discretion in the hands of the tax officer, high stakes, sky high stakes, you're talking thousands of crore rupees for big accounts, and uh complete opacity. So horrible problem, four on four.

core_ideas.concept: The Hacking Mindset: Redesign a Hard Problem into an Easy One
core_ideas.explanation: Difficulty is often a product of institutional design. Monetary policy was once an opaque, high-discretion domain ruled by a powerful governor. An inflation target, a committee dominated by private economists, and full transparency 'hacked the components' to make it easy. IT can do the same: computerisation tames high transaction volumes, and open databases strip frontline discretion, as with railway reservations. Facing a bad row in the table, ask which metric you can flip by redesign.
core_ideas.quote: So we changed our whole paradigm of how to think about this in order to make it easy.

core_ideas.explanation: A finance person may find banking regulation easy because it is familiar, and monetary policy mysterious because it is alien. Neither feeling says anything about real difficulty; unfamiliarity only means you need the right expertise. A shared, explicit framework removes this bias and gives people a common language to argue in. Amit adds that even imperfect measurement sharpens thinking: 'Not everything is precisely measurable, but the more you attempt to measure something, the more clarity you gain in thinking about it.'
core_ideas.quote: So this protects us from our own vulgar familiarity, and it gives us a more objective way to rate the complexity of alternative problems.

core_ideas.concept: Adam Smith's Essentials Are the Hardest Problems
core_ideas.explanation: Smith said little else is needed for opulence but peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice. Run these through the four metrics. Peace (military, police, criminal justice), taxes and courts are all brutally hard. So the minimal state is not an easy state. Capability has a budget constraint: money, civil servant headcount, and above all the attention of leaders, researchers and reform teams. A chief minister's calendar decides what gets done. This is why mission creep is so costly: every extra project drains the core, which may take 50 to 100 years to get right.
core_ideas.quote: So suddenly we get a new insight into the world that little else is required, but what is required is very, very hard.

core_ideas.concept: Hard Is Not the Same as Unimportant
core_ideas.explanation: The four metrics measure difficulty, not importance. Smith's three essentials are both necessary and practically sufficient, so they must be done however hard they are. The danger is drifting toward easy, inconsequential problems that don't move the needle, as in the lamppost parable.
core_ideas.quote: the metrics that we laid out are not metrics for importance, they're metrics for how hard something is. And just because something is very hard doesn't mean that it should not be done.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit borrows Francis Fukuyama's distinction. Scope is how many things a state does, and strength is how well it does them. The Indian state is high on scope and low on strength. The four metrics explain why the fix is hard: the few things a state must do well are exactly the hardest ones, so the state has to narrow its scope to build strength.
core_ideas.quote: Now both you and I agree that what the Indian State should do is it should do a few things well, not many things badly.

core_ideas.concept: The Two Exit Ramps from Hard Work
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's classification of how policymakers dodge the hard core. The first is welfareism: humanitarian projects that bring the satisfaction of having fed some children lunch without touching the hard problems. The second is the engineer's ramp: build an app or website, hold an inauguration, celebrate, and achieve nothing. In their book, Kelkar and Shah title a section 'Everybody Loves a Good IT System', riffing on P. Sainath.
core_ideas.quote: Some software vendor builds an app, some software vendor builds a website, you celebrate, you'll inaugurate it, nothing will get done.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit opens in the dark ('I don't know if you can see us') and turns it into a parable: 'We are shrouded in darkness today. The light of freedom has gone out of our lives. Everyone thought intervention will show us a way... but instead it burnt everything to the ground and there is no power anymore.'

After Ajay says Lant Pritchett would agree that their extended version is better, Amit plugs his Seen and the Unseen episodes. Ajay now has fourteen, 'tied with our good friend Pranay Kotasthane... it's a good battle who's gonna win.'
Amit on Ajay's academic standards: 'I told you, hey, don't bring your paperwala goals to the show... So I'm very happy for you, finally an episode with novel insights.'

Ajay says this kind of feasibility conversation is 'conspicuously absent' in Indian public affairs. Amit: 'Actually, it is conspicuously absent only now that we have brought it to people's attention. Before this it was unconspicuously absent because nobody knew it was missing. Words matter.'
Amit uses the writing-workshop rule on Ajay to ask for examples: 'I'm gonna do the writer thing and tell you now. Don't tell me, show me, show, don't tell.'
Ajay's teacher-discretion example asks 'Do I teach to the genius Amit Varma in my front row...?' Amit protests: 'I was always a backbencher... I never sat on a front bench.'
Amit, delighted with the difficulty table: 'I want you to build tables like this for me in every area of my life, so all my decision making becomes easy.'

In the lamppost parable Amit stresses this is 'a good policeman in a country with rule of law' who helps 'with great humility and a sense of service'. He also declares that the tough, fuzzy problems are 'what a real man tries to solve and Lant Pritchett is a real man.'
Ajay on government IT launches: 'you celebrate, you'll inaugurate it, nothing will get done... No one was saved. Eleanor Rigby.' Amit signs off: 'We've got a Beatles song about IT systems.'

Adam Smith, which Ajay calls one of the greatest quotes in economics: 'little else is requisite to carry a state to the highest degree of opulence from the lowest barbarism, but peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice. All the rest being brought about by the natural course of things.'
P. Sainath's book 'Everybody Loves a Good Drought', which Kelkar and Shah riff on in a section titled 'Everybody Loves a Good IT System'.
Francis Fukuyama's distinction between the scope of a state (how many things it does) and its strength (how well it does them).
Jawaharlal Nehru in 1947, imagined brushing off Smith's three essentials in favour of land reform.

Transparency institutions as checks on the state: 'just imagine if there was no CAG, if there was no RTI... then like anything can be done.' Also the Indian Financial Code drafted by FSLRC, cited as the kind of properly drafted law that makes inflation targeting easy to roll out.

Yuen Yuen Ang's 'Adaptive Political Economy' uses the same drunk-under-the-lamppost metaphor that Amit used to open his Lant Pritchett episode. Amit says she will be on The Seen and the Unseen once she finishes a very important book she is writing.
